newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: COSTELLO SAYS MOMENTUM FOR TAX REFORM UNDENIABLE
Federal Treasurer, Peter Costello, says it is time Australia embarked on a serious debate about reforming the taxation system, which he described as inefficient and unsustainable.
Mr Costello says the debate about the merits of a consumption tax will not go away, and has urged his colleagues to canvass opinion on the issue in their electorates.
Coalition MPs met in Canberra last night to discuss taxation reform.
Mr Costello says the meeting expressed a genuine desire for change.
He says the debate is a complicated one, but it affects everyone, and so will not go away.
The Treasurer says the current tax base will not last into the next century, and needs to be improved.
But he says it will be important to garner public support before moving to reform the system, because people will welcome change if they believe there is a problem that needs fixing.
WEATHER PATTERNS CREATE GRIM FORECAST FOR RURAL EXPORTS

Australia's drier than usual weather conditions could cost the country more than $1 billion dollars in farm export revenue. The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics predicts grain crops will be most affected, with the possibility that the winter wheat harvest could fall by 30 percent on last year.
The Bureau also says a continuing dry winter and poor pasture conditions will most likely result in an increased turnoff of sheep and cattle.
ABARE's chief commodity analyst Terry Sheales says that could reduce overall export earnings by 5-percent to $20.2 Billion dollars.
However, ABARE has positive predictions for coal and wool.
The bureau expects a significant recovery in wool prices, with a rise in demand for fine wool as well, particularly in Italy.
Coal exports are also expected to rise by 35 percent in the next five years, with 11 new mines in Queensland, and 15 in New South Wales.
OPPOSITION TO JABILUKA PLAN STILL STRONG
The Australian Democrats are querying the claims of the company proposing the Jabiluka uranium mine in Kakadu National Park, that it has an environmentally-clean record.
Both the Democrats and the Greens are urging the Federal Government to reject the proposed mine, which they claim would impact on Kakadu and the traditional owners.

Mining company, Energy Resources of Australia, is resting its case for an underground mine with uranium ore trucked to the existing Ranger mine for processing, on its 16-year environmental record at Ranger.
Federal Environment Minister Robert Hill has received a final environmental impact statement on the project, but the Democrats are questioning the company's record.
Democrats environment spokesman Meg Lees says Jabiluka is unacceptable in any form, while Greens senator Dee Margetts wants the government to refuse to grant export licences.
PAYBACK DEFENDED BY ABORIGINAL LEADER
An Aboriginal leader in Central Australia has called on the Western legal system to recognise the importance of traditional payback.
Justice Sir William Kearney said in the Northern Territory Supreme Court last week payback should not be tolerated, and the sooner it was stamped out, the better.
But senior Walpiri man, Harry Jagamurra Nelson says the court should change to recognise traditional law and culture.
Mr Nelson says if the payback is conducted within white laws, and it is done correctly, the police should not be involved.
ALLEGATIONS ILLEGAL ARRIVALS LINKED TO ORGANISED CRIME
Immigration Minister Philip Ruddock says he can't confirm any connection between organised crime and the illegal entry of 139 people into Australia last week.
He says he can't comment on allegations about the nature of the party, other than to say that the circumstances and its method of arrival were very unusual.
The group was captured in Australian waters after arriving by boat in the Torres Strait Islands on Australia's eastern coast last Friday.
Independent MP Grahame Campbell, claimed in Parliament today they've come from Fujian province in China and their arrival suggests Australia is being targetted by organised crime.
Mr Ruddock told Parliament the vessel was especially acquired for the journey and its passengers presented differently to others attempting to enter Australia in the same way.
